6Understand What Brands And Clients Look For

Before you create content, it helps to know what people who pay look for. Understanding this shapes everything you do.

What brands usually look for

Brands that work with creators typically care about:

  • A clear niche and audience that matches their customers.
  • Engagement, meaning people actually respond to your content, more than a big follower count.
  • Content quality, which means clear visuals, good light and clear sound, not an expensive camera.
  • Reliability and professionalism. Do you reply, meet deadlines and follow briefs?
  • Authenticity. Do you appear to genuinely use and like products like theirs?
  • A clean history. No fake followers, no purchased engagement, no scandals.
  • The ability to follow rules, such as clearly disclosing partnerships.

What clients look for when hiring you for a service

If you are offering a service, such as social media management or content creation, clients look for:

  • A profile that clearly says what you do and who you do it for.
  • Examples of your work and results.
  • Testimonials or comments from satisfied people.
  • A simple way to contact and book you.
  • Proof that you are consistent.

Fake followers and purchased engagement: please do not

You will see ads for buying followers and likes. Do not. Fake followers do not buy anything, brands can often spot them and your engagement rate collapses. Instagram may also penalise accounts for it. Build slowly and honestly. Real, small audiences outperform fake, large ones every time.

Small is not a disadvantage

A smaller account with a tight niche and an active audience can be more valuable to some brands than a huge, scattered one. People call accounts with smaller, highly engaged audiences by names such as nano or micro creators, and some brands deliberately look for them because their recommendations feel personal. Terms and thresholds vary, so do not worry about the labels. Worry about clarity and trust.

7Your Toolkit

You do not need a studio. You need a phone, some free tools and good habits. Check current features, limits and prices on every tool before you rely on it.

The free starter kit

What you needFree option to start with
Filming and photosYour phone's camera, with a clean lens and natural light
Basic video editingInstagram's own editor, or a free mobile editing app
Graphics and carouselsA free design tool with templates
Captions on videoInstagram's captions feature or a free captioning app
PlanningA notes app, spreadsheet or free calendar
Link in bio pageA free link page tool, or a simple one-page site
AnalyticsInstagram's built-in insights
SchedulingInstagram's own scheduling feature, where available
Tracking moneyA free spreadsheet
SecurityA password manager and two-step verification

Cheap gear that actually helps

If you want to spend a little, these upgrades matter most, in this order:

1. Light. A window is free. A small ring light or lamp is inexpensive. 2. Sound. A simple clip-on microphone makes a bigger difference than a fancier camera. 3. Stability. A small tripod or phone stand lets you film hands-free. 4. Backdrop. A plain wall, a neat shelf or a clean sheet is enough.

Do not buy gear before you have a posting habit. Equipment does not create consistency.

Using AI tools wisely

AI assistants can help you brainstorm ideas, draft captions, suggest hooks and summarise your insights. They are useful assistants, not replacements for your voice. Always rewrite in your own words, check facts and never paste private information about yourself, clients or brands into a tool unless you have checked its privacy rules. For a deeper guide, see How To Use ChatGPT And Claude To Build Real Income Streams. You can also try the free AI Prompt Builder.

Tracking sheet

Create one spreadsheet with tabs for content ideas, posting calendar, outreach, income and learning notes. We will use it throughout this guide. Keep it simple.

8Build A Content System You Can Sustain

Most accounts that earn do not have more talent. They have a system. A content system is a repeatable way to come up with ideas, create content and post it, without starting from zero each day. Here is how to build one.

Step one: choose your content pillars

Content pillars are the three to five themes you will return to again and again. They make planning easy and make your account feel clear.

Example for a budget meals account, made up:

1. Quick recipes under twenty minutes. 2. Shopping and saving tips. 3. Kitchen hacks for small spaces. 4. Honest product reviews. 5. Behind the scenes and personal stories.

Write yours. Each pillar should connect to your niche and to something your audience needs.

Step two: learn the main formats and what they are good for

Reels are short vertical videos. They are the main route to reach people who do not follow you yet. Keep them clear and quick, with a strong opening.

Carousels are swipeable slide posts. They are great for teaching, step-by-step guides, lists and checklists, and they are easy to save and share.

Single images work for quotes, announcements and simple tips.

Stories are for daily connection: polls, questions, behind-the-scenes and links.

Lives are real-time videos where you can talk to your audience. Useful once you have a regular audience.

A simple starting mix for many accounts: a few reels a week, one or two carousels and daily stories when you can. Adjust to what you can sustain.

Step three: generate ideas without staring at a blank screen

Use these idea sources:

  • Questions. Every question your audience asks, in comments, messages and polls, is a post.
  • Problems. What frustrates your ideal follower? Each frustration is a post.
  • Your own experience. What did you learn this week? What mistake did you make?
  • Myths. "People think X, but actually Y."
  • Step-by-step. "How to do [small task] in three steps."
  • Before and after. Show a change.
  • Lists. "Five things I wish I knew about [topic]."
  • Reviews and comparisons. Honest opinions on products you really use.
  • Behind the scenes. Show your process.
  • Seasonal moments. Holidays, school terms and events relevant to your niche.

Aim for a bank of thirty ideas. Keep them in your tracking sheet and add to it whenever one appears.

Step four: write strong hooks

A hook is the first line or the first second that makes someone stop scrolling. Most people decide within moments whether to keep watching.

Hook formulas that work in many niches:

  • The promise: "How to cook dinner in fifteen minutes with three ingredients."
  • The mistake: "The biggest mistake I made when I started budgeting."
  • The question: "Do you also forget to eat until three in the afternoon?"
  • The surprising fact: "You can save money on groceries without buying cheaper food."
  • The list: "Five free tools every beginner needs."
  • The story: "Last week, a brand told me no, and here is what I learned."

A good hook is honest. If your video does not deliver on the promise, people feel tricked and leave.

Step five: structure your content

A simple structure for a short video or carousel:

1. Hook: stop the scroll. 2. Value: deliver one clear idea, tip or story. 3. Proof or example: show it working. 4. Call to action: tell people what to do next, such as save, share or message you.

One idea per post. If you cram in three, people remember none.

Step six: write captions that work

Captions give context and invite action. Keep the first line strong, because it shows before the "more" button. Use short paragraphs, plain words and a clear call to action. Ask a genuine question to start a conversation. Add keywords naturally, since Instagram search uses words in captions and profiles. Avoid walls of text, and proofread.

Step seven: use hashtags and keywords sensibly

Hashtags and keywords help Instagram understand what your content is about. Use a small number of relevant ones, rather than dozens of random ones. Mix very specific tags with broader ones related to your niche. Platform advice about hashtags changes, so check current guidance, and watch your own insights to see what brings people to your content.

Step eight: batch your creation

Batching means doing the same type of task for many posts at once. Instead of creating one post every day, set aside a block of time to do each stage for several posts.

A simple weekly batching rhythm:

  • Planning (thirty minutes): choose the week's ideas and write hooks.
  • Filming or designing (one to two hours): record several videos and design carousels in one session. Change tops or backgrounds to create variety.
  • Editing and captions (one hour): edit, add captions and write the post text.
  • Scheduling (fifteen minutes): schedule posts for the week using Instagram's scheduling tool or a calendar reminder.
  • Engagement (fifteen minutes a day): reply to comments and messages, and interact with other accounts.

You can make this fit around work or study. Two short sessions a week can be enough.

Step nine: choose a posting rhythm you can keep

Consistency matters more than frequency. Three posts a week for six months beats daily posting for two weeks followed by silence. Choose a rhythm you can honestly keep when you are tired, and write it down. For example: "Three reels, one carousel, stories on weekdays."

Step ten: engage, do not just broadcast

Instagram is social. After you post, spend a few minutes replying to comments. Visit accounts in your niche and leave genuine, thoughtful comments, not "nice pic." Answer direct messages kindly. Engagement signals to the platform that your content is worth showing and builds real relationships with brands and followers.

A simple daily routine, fifteen to twenty minutes:

1. Reply to all comments on your latest post. 2. Check and reply to direct messages. 3. Leave five thoughtful comments on posts in your niche. 4. Post or share a story.

Step eleven: review your insights weekly

Once a week, open your insights and note:

  • Which posts got the most saves and shares?
  • Which got the most new followers?
  • What times and days did your audience respond best?
  • What topics and formats worked?

Write three lines: what to do more of, what to do less of and what to try next week. This simple review is how accounts improve.

A sample week of content, made up

DayContentPillar
MondayReel: 15-minute pasta with three ingredientsQuick recipes
TuesdayStories: poll on favourite cheap mealsBehind the scenes
WednesdayCarousel: five ways to cut your grocery billShopping and saving
ThursdayReel: small kitchen hackKitchen hacks
FridayStories: weekly question boxEngagement
SaturdayReel: honest review of a kitchen toolReviews
SundayRest and plan next weekPlanning

What to do if you run out of ideas

Reuse and repurpose. Turn a popular reel into a carousel. Turn a carousel into a series of stories. Answer a comment with a whole post. Revisit older topics with new angles. Update posts that performed well. Repetition is not boring to people who have not seen it yet.

9Follow The Rules And Stay Honest

Trust is your most valuable asset, and rules protect it. A few important principles, but please check the rules in your own country, because I am not a lawyer.

Disclose partnerships

In many countries, the law requires you to make it clear when you have been paid, given free products or have another connection to a brand you promote. Instagram provides a paid partnership label and tools for this. Use them. Add clear wording such as "ad" or "paid partnership" where appropriate. Hiding it can damage trust and can break rules or laws. Check your country's advertising guidelines.

Be honest about products

Only recommend what you have genuinely used or have good reason to believe in. Never invent results, testimonials or medical or financial claims. Be especially careful in areas like health, supplements, weight loss, skincare claims and money, because rules and consequences can be serious.

Respect copyright

Do not use other people's photos, videos, text or music without permission or a proper licence. Instagram has libraries of audio for certain accounts, and some music is restricted for business accounts, so check what you can use. Free design tools have licence rules for images and fonts, so read them. Copyright takedowns can remove your content or harm your account.

Respect privacy

Ask before filming or posting other people, especially children. Do not share private conversations, addresses or personal details. Do not post client information without permission.

Follow Instagram's community rules

Read the platform's current guidelines. Accounts that break them may be limited or removed, and rebuilding is hard.

Keep an archive

Back up your best content and your account details. If something goes wrong, you will be glad you did. Keep screenshots of important messages and agreements.

Pro Tip 💡 The safest rule is simple: if you would be embarrassed to explain it to a brand, a follower or your future self, do not do it.

10A Closer Look: How To Make A Reel From Start To Finish

Reels are often the main way strangers discover you, so let us slow down and walk through one properly. You can do all of this with a phone.

Step one: choose one idea and one viewer

Pick a single idea from your bank, and imagine your ideal follower watching it. "Three free tools for planning a month of content" is one idea. "Everything about growing on Instagram" is far too big for one reel.

Step two: write a tiny script

A reel does not need a long script, but a few lines help you avoid rambling. Write:

1. The hook (one sentence, spoken or written on screen). 2. The three beats (the three tips, steps or moments). 3. The close (a call to action, such as "save this for later" or "follow for more").

A made-up script for a budget meals account: "Hook: This dinner costs less than a bus ride. Beat one: cook pasta. Beat two: fry garlic and tomatoes. Beat three: mix and top with cheese. Close: save this for your next tight week."

Step three: set up your space

Face a window or a lamp so light falls on your face or your product. Clean the camera lens. Use a plain background. Prop your phone on a stack of books or a small tripod. Keep your phone in vertical mode. Film a few seconds of silence at the start so your edit is cleaner.

Step four: film in small clips

Film each beat separately, two or three takes each. Speak clearly and a little slower than you would in conversation. Show hands and products clearly. Do not worry about perfection. Natural is more relatable than polished.

Step five: edit simply

Trim the start so the hook appears immediately. Cut pauses and repeated lines. Add on-screen text for the hook and key points. Add captions so people can follow with the sound off. Keep the video as short as it needs to be to deliver the idea.

Step six: choose sound carefully

Sound matters, but so does permission. Use audio that Instagram allows for your account type, or music you have the right to use. Business accounts often have restrictions on commercial music, so check what is available. Clear speech with low background noise beats a trendy track you cannot use.

Step seven: write the caption and add a call to action

Write a caption that adds something the video did not, such as a tip or a short story. Add a clear call to action. Add a few relevant keywords or hashtags.

Step eight: post and engage

Post at a time when your audience is active, if your insights show it. Reply to every comment in the first hour if you can. Share the reel to your story with a prompt like "Which one would you try?"

Step nine: learn from it

After a day or two, look at the insights. Did people watch to the end? Did they save or share? Where did they stop watching? If many leave in the first seconds, strengthen your hook. If they watch but do not follow, strengthen your profile and call to action.

Hook bank for any niche

Copy and adapt these. Replace the brackets with your topic.

  • "Stop doing [common mistake] if you want [result]."
  • "I tried [thing] for [time], and here is what happened."
  • "Three things I wish I knew before [starting something]."
  • "If you only have [limited time or money], do this."
  • "The easiest way to [result] without [common pain]."
  • "Nobody tells you this about [topic]."
  • "Here is how I would [achieve result] if I were starting again."
  • "Save this if you are struggling with [problem]."

11A Closer Look: A Weekly Growth Routine

Growth is not a trick. It is a rhythm repeated for months. Here is a simple, honest routine.

Monday: plan. Choose your three to five ideas for the week. Write hooks and one-line scripts.

Tuesday: create. Batch film and design. Aim for a few pieces.

Wednesday: edit and schedule. Add captions, check disclosure where needed and schedule.

Thursday and Friday: engage and learn. Reply to comments, message, comment on others' content and read your insights.

Saturday: connect. Message or collaborate with one creator or business. Share a story with a question or poll.

Sunday: review and rest. Write down what worked and what did not, then switch off.

Profile audit: fifteen quick checks

Once a month, look at your own profile as if you were a brand seeing it for the first time.

1. Is my username easy to say and spell? 2. Does my name field say what I do? 3. Is my photo clear when small? 4. Does my bio say who I help and what to do next? 5. Is my link working and loading quickly? 6. Is there a way to contact me? 7. Do my first nine posts look consistent? 8. Do they clearly show my niche? 9. Do my highlights explain who I am and how to work with me? 10. Have I posted recently and consistently? 11. Do I reply to comments and messages? 12. Are my captions clear and free of mistakes? 13. Do I disclose partnerships clearly? 14. Is my account secure, with two-step verification on? 15. Would a brand quickly understand why I am a fit?

Fix one or two things each month.

Collaboration that helps both accounts

Collaborating with creators at a similar stage is a gentle, honest way to grow. Ideas: a shared reel where each of you gives one tip, a live conversation about a topic, a "swap" where you each answer the other's audience questions or a joint giveaway where rules and prizes are clear and legal in your country. Choose partners whose values and audience match yours, and agree on the details in writing.

12A Closer Look: Thirty Content Prompts For Any Niche

If you are staring at a blank page, work through these prompts. Each can become a reel, carousel or story. Replace the brackets with your own niche.

1. The three questions I get asked most about [topic]. 2. A myth about [topic] and what is true. 3. My morning or daily routine for [topic]. 4. A mistake I made when I started [topic]. 5. A tool I use every day for [topic], and why. 6. A free alternative to something expensive in [topic]. 7. A simple step-by-step for [small task]. 8. A before and after related to [topic]. 9. My honest opinion on a popular [product or trend]. 10. How much time I spend on [topic] each week. 11. A quick win anyone can do in ten minutes. 12. Something I stopped doing and what changed. 13. A common beginner mistake and how to fix it. 14. A checklist for [situation]. 15. Five things in my bag, kitchen, desk or routine. 16. A story about a time something went wrong and what I learned. 17. A reaction to a common piece of advice. 18. A comparison between two options in [topic]. 19. A day in my life as someone learning [topic]. 20. A reply to a follower's question. 21. A list of the resources I use to learn. 22. A small goal I am working on and how I will track it. 23. A seasonal tip for [topic]. 24. What I would buy, and not buy, with a small budget. 25. A behind-the-scenes look at making a post. 26. A free resource or template I made. 27. A question to start a conversation. 28. A review of a book, course or product I have used. 29. A "start here" post for new followers. 30. A thank-you to my community and what is next.

Caption templates

Use these structures and fill in your own words.

The teaching caption. First line: the promise. Middle: three short steps. End: a question or a call to save.

The story caption. First line: a moment ("Last week I almost gave up."). Middle: what happened and what you learned. End: a takeaway and a question.

The offer caption. First line: the problem. Middle: how your service or product helps and who it is for. End: a clear next step, such as "Message me the word PLAN."

The review caption. First line: your honest verdict. Middle: what you liked, what you did not and who it suits. End: disclosure if relevant and a question.

13A Sample Media Kit, Written Out

Here is a made-up media kit in text form, so you can picture what to include. Replace everything with your own honest information.

Ruth Eze | Skincare for Dry Skin Instagram: @ruthskincare | Email: ruth@example.com

About me. I share honest, simple skincare tips and product reviews for women with dry skin. My style is calm, clear and practical. I only recommend products I have used for at least two weeks.

My audience. About [number] followers. Most are women aged [range] based in [countries]. My average engagement rate over the last ten posts is [number] percent, based on likes, comments, saves and shares divided by followers. My audience most often saves ingredient guides and routine posts.

What I offer.

  • One short video with captions.
  • A set of three to five stories.
  • A carousel on ingredients or routines.
  • UGC videos for your own channels.
  • Usage rights options, with prices available on request.

Past work and results. [List a couple of examples, such as a practice collaboration or a sample, labelled honestly, with what the post achieved.]

How I work. I read the brief carefully, send drafts for approval when agreed, disclose all partnerships clearly and deliver on time.

What I will not promote. Products that make unsafe health claims or that I would not use myself.

Contact. Email me to discuss a collaboration, and I will send my rates.

Keep it to one or two pages with a clean layout. Update it every few months.

14Route One: Earn From Services

This is the most reliable beginner route, because you do not need a big following. You need a skill that a small business values, and a profile that shows it. Almost every small business is on Instagram, and many are struggling to keep their pages active.

Services people hire beginners for

  • Social media management. Planning, designing and scheduling posts for small businesses.
  • Content creation. Photos, short videos or graphics.
  • Caption and copywriting. Writing captions, bios and product descriptions.
  • Virtual assistance. Replying to messages, scheduling and organising for busy business owners. See Pretty, Paid And Booked.
  • Design. Templates, highlight covers, carousels and simple brand kits.
  • Editing. Trimming and captioning short videos for busy creators.
  • Community management. Replying to comments and messages on a business account, within clear guidelines.
  • Coaching or teaching. Helping beginners with skills you have, such as budgeting, studying or planning.

For a fuller walk-through of finding and winning clients, read How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

Build a simple service offer

A clear offer is a small package that someone can say yes to in one sentence. Use this structure:

What I do, for whom, what is included and what it costs.

Examples, all made up:

  • "I design and schedule twelve Instagram posts a month for small salons. Includes captions and a monthly summary."
  • "I film and edit three short product videos for small skincare brands, with captions."
  • "I write a month of captions and a posting plan for small food businesses."

Keep it specific, and put a clear price. Research what is fair in your market, since rates differ widely. The free Freelance Rate Calculator can help you think it through.

Show your work on your profile

Make it obvious that you offer services. Put your service in your name field or bio. Create highlights called "Work with me" and "Results." Share short case notes: what a client needed, what you did and what happened, without sharing private details. Use before-and-after posts when you have permission. Ask happy clients for short testimonials and, with their permission, share them.

Find your first clients

  • Your warm network. People you already know may need help or know someone who does.
  • Local businesses. Search for businesses in your town, notice ones with inconsistent posting and contact them politely.
  • Your own audience. Mention that you take a limited number of clients. Some followers may be business owners.
  • Comments and conversations. Leave thoughtful comments on business accounts in your area. Do not pitch in comments, but be visible and helpful.
  • Referrals. Ask every happy client who else might need your help.

We will cover exactly what to say in the scripts chapter.

Offer a small, limited sample

A small free sample can help a hesitant business owner trust you, such as three designed posts or a short page review. Keep it clearly limited, set a deadline and agree in writing what you are offering. Do not give away unlimited free work.

Protect yourself

Confirm the work in writing: what you will deliver, by when, the price, how many changes are included and how you will be paid. Never ask for a client's personal passwords. Use proper tools that let you manage a page with permission, and remind clients they can remove your access at any time. For more, read How To Get Paid As A Freelancer.

15Route Two: Earn From UGC

UGC stands for user-generated content. In this model, brands pay you to create photos or videos that they will use on their own channels, such as their website, adverts or social pages. You might not even post it on your own account. That is why this route suits people with small or private accounts.

Why brands pay for UGC

Many people trust content from a real person more than a polished advert. Brands need a steady supply of fresh, relatable content, and creating it in-house is expensive. So they hire everyday creators who can film a clear, appealing video on a phone.

What UGC creators actually do

  • Film short videos that show a product being used, with a clear hook and honest reaction.
  • Take photos of products in natural settings.
  • Follow a brief, which is a short document telling you what the brand wants.
  • Deliver files on time, in the format requested.
  • Sometimes provide a script or voiceover.

Skills you need

You do not need a huge following. You need to be able to film in good light, speak clearly, hold a product steadily, follow instructions and keep to deadlines. All of these are learnable. Practise with products you already own.

Build a UGC portfolio

You need samples. Create three to five practice pieces using products you already have, such as a skincare product, a kitchen item or a notebook. Make a short video with a hook, a demonstration and a closing line. Make a few photos with clean backgrounds. Collect them in a simple portfolio page or a folder with a public link. Label them honestly as sample or practice content.

Where UGC work comes from

  • Direct outreach. Contact small brands with a short, personal pitch and your samples. We will give you scripts.
  • Marketplaces and platforms. Some websites connect brands with creators. Read the terms and fees, and check current options.
  • Brand job posts. Brands sometimes post on social media or job boards that they need creators.
  • Referrals. Happy brands recommend you.

Pricing UGC

Prices differ widely by market, brand size and what is included. Think about:

  • Time. How long does it take to plan, film, edit and revise?
  • Deliverables. How many videos or photos?
  • Usage rights. What can the brand do with your content, for how long and where? Using your work in paid adverts is often worth more than organic posts.
  • Exclusivity. Are you barred from working with similar brands for a period?
  • Revisions. How many changes are included?
  • Turnaround. Rush jobs usually cost more.

Create a simple rate card with a price for each deliverable and add-ons for extras such as extended usage rights. Start with a fair, modest price, and raise it as your portfolio and speed grow.

UGC contracts and usage rights

Always agree the terms in writing. Make sure you understand what rights the brand gets and for how long, whether you may also post the content, and when and how you will be paid. If a contract grants rights forever for no extra payment, think carefully. I am not a lawyer, so for anything significant, ask a qualified person or check your local rules.

16Route Three: Earn From Brand Partnerships

This is the route most people imagine when they say "make money on Instagram." It is real, but it often comes after you have built trust and a clear niche. It is also the route with the most scams, so we will go carefully.

The types of brand deals

Gifted collaboration. A brand sends you a product and asks you to feature it. You are not paid in money. Many beginners start here. Be careful: free products are not a salary, and you should only accept things you genuinely want and are willing to talk about. You still need to disclose that the product was gifted, according to the rules in your country.

Paid post or video. A brand pays you a fee to create content that features them. This is the classic sponsored post.

Ambassador arrangement. An ongoing relationship over weeks or months, usually with several pieces of content.

Affiliate-based deal. You earn a commission on sales rather than a fixed fee.

Hybrid deal. A combination, such as a small fee plus commission.

Who gets brand deals?

Brands choose creators whose audience matches their customers, who create good content and who behave professionally. Small accounts can win deals, especially with small and local brands, new brands and brands that value niche audiences. Large brands often work through agencies and have stricter requirements.

Preparing to pitch

Before you contact any brand, make sure you have:

  • A clear profile with a clear niche and contact details.
  • At least a dozen good posts that show your style and quality.
  • Some evidence of engagement, such as comments and saves.
  • A simple media kit.
  • A basic rate card.

How to build a media kit

A media kit is a one- or two-page document that tells a brand who you are. Keep it clean and honest. Include:

1. Your name, handle, photo and contact details. 2. A short bio: who you are, your niche and your style. 3. Your audience: follower count, engagement rate, top locations, age range and gender split if you know them from your insights. Be honest and accurate. 4. Your content: two or three best examples with a short note on results, such as saves or comments, if you have them. 5. Services and rates: a short list of what you offer. You can say "rates on request" if you prefer, but be ready to share them. 6. Past work or testimonials, if you have them. 7. Your values or what you will not promote.

Design it in a free design tool and export it as a PDF. Update it every few months with fresh numbers. Never inflate your statistics. Brands can check, and lying ends relationships.

Calculate your engagement rate

A simple way: take the total likes, comments, saves and shares on a recent post, divide by your follower count and multiply by one hundred. Do it for your last ten posts and average them. Example, made up: if ten posts averaged forty interactions and you have eight hundred followers, that is five percent. Different brands use different formulas, so be clear about how you calculated yours.

Finding brands that fit

  • Look at the brands you already use and love. Authenticity shows.
  • Look at the brands that your ideal follower uses.
  • Look at brands that already work with creators like you, and note which ones appear repeatedly.
  • Search for small and local businesses in your niche. They often have flexibility and welcome fresh creators.
  • Check brand pages for a "collaborations" or "partnerships" section, or a contact email.

Make a list of twenty brands. For each, note why they fit, who to contact and what you could offer.

How to pitch, in short

A good pitch is short, personal and focused on what the brand gets. It includes who you are, why you are writing to this brand specifically, what you propose and a simple next step. Keep it under about a hundred and fifty words. We will give you complete scripts in the scripts chapter.

Pricing a brand partnership

Pricing is one of the hardest parts, so let us make it practical. Think in layers.

1. Your time. Planning, creating, editing, posting and replying. 2. The deliverables. A reel, a carousel, stories, a set of photos. 3. Usage rights. Will the brand reuse your content in adverts or on their site? 4. Exclusivity. Will you be barred from working with competitors? 5. Your audience's value. An engaged, niche audience is worth more than a large, passive one. 6. The market. Check what similar creators with similar audiences charge, and keep in mind your country.

A common starting approach is to calculate a fair hourly value for your time, multiply by the hours the project will take, then add a fee for usage rights and exclusivity where relevant. You can use the free Freelance Rate Calculator to get started. Rate guides online vary enormously, so treat any single "rate per follower" formula with caution.

Negotiating, calmly

When a brand makes an offer, you do not have to say yes or no immediately. You can say, "Thank you, I would love to work together. Let me review the details and get back to you." If the offer is lower than you want, you can propose adjustments: a higher fee, fewer deliverables, a shorter usage period or additional payment for extended rights. Keep your tone warm and professional. If the budget is firm and too low, it is fine to decline politely.

The agreement

For any paid partnership, get the main terms in writing: what you will deliver, the dates, the fee, payment date and method, usage rights, exclusivity, approval and revision process and what happens if either side cancels. For bigger deals, ask for a proper contract, and read it carefully. I am not a lawyer, so for important agreements, please get advice.

Delivering well

Read the brief carefully. Ask questions early. Send drafts for approval if agreed. Disclose the partnership clearly. Post on time. Share results afterwards, such as views and saves, with a short thank-you note. Brands remember creators who are easy to work with, and repeat work is where the real money often is.

Getting paid

Send an invoice with your details, the brand's details, the deliverables, the amount, the date and payment instructions. Follow up politely if payment is late. Never post content before the agreed deposit or payment arrives if your agreement says otherwise. Keep records of every payment for taxes, and check your local rules.

17Route Four: Affiliate Income

Affiliate marketing means you recommend a product or service, and if someone buys through your special link, you earn a commission. You are not employed by the company. You are rewarded for referrals.

How it works, step by step

1. A company runs an affiliate programme, either directly or through an affiliate network. 2. You apply or sign up, and receive a unique link or code. 3. You share that link or code when you genuinely recommend the product. 4. Someone clicks and buys. 5. The company's system tracks it and pays you a commission, usually after a set period.

What to promote

Choose products that:

  • You have actually used and can speak about honestly.
  • Solve a real problem your audience has.
  • Come from trustworthy companies with clear terms and reasonable refund policies.
  • Offer fair commissions and reliable payment.

Avoid products that make exaggerated promises, pay unclear commissions or require you to recruit others. Be very careful with anything that sounds like a pyramid scheme, where income depends on recruiting rather than selling a real product.

Where to find affiliate programmes

Many brands list their affiliate programme on their website, often in the footer. Some use affiliate networks that bring many brands together. Check the terms, payment threshold, payout schedule and country eligibility before you sign up. Programmes and rules change, so read the current terms.

How to share affiliate links on Instagram

Instagram does not make every link clickable in captions, so creators often use their link in bio, link pages or direct messages, depending on what is currently allowed. A common method is: post helpful content, invite people to message you a keyword and send the link in a reply. Check current features and rules, since Instagram's policies about links and automated messages change.

Disclose, always

Clearly say when a link is an affiliate link. Use plain wording such as "affiliate link" or "I earn a small commission." Many countries require this. It also builds trust, because people respect honesty.

Make helpful content, not sales pitches

The most effective affiliate content teaches. For example: "My three favourite free tools for planning a month of content" with honest notes on each, and a link for those who want to try them. Show how you actually use the product. Mention downsides honestly. People trust balanced opinions.

Realistic expectations

Affiliate income usually starts small, and it grows with trust and audience size. A single post is unlikely to change your life. A library of helpful content, shared consistently, may bring steady small commissions over time. Treat it as one stream among several.

18Route Five: Your Own Digital Products

A digital product is something you create once and can sell many times, delivered electronically. Examples: a planner, a template pack, a checklist bundle, a guide or a small course. Instagram is a wonderful place to sell them, because you can teach for free and then offer a deeper version.

Why digital products suit Instagram

You already create helpful content. A product packages that help in a more complete, convenient form. Your audience already trusts you, so the step to buying is smaller.

Ideas by niche, all made up

  • A budget niche: a monthly budget planner spreadsheet.
  • A food niche: a printable weekly meal planner and shopping list.
  • A study niche: a revision timetable template.
  • A business niche: a client onboarding checklist for freelancers.
  • A skincare niche: a simple routine tracker.
  • A planning niche: a content calendar template for small businesses.

How to create one, step by step

1. Find a repeated question. What do people keep asking you? 2. Choose a clear promise. "A one-page weekly meal plan that takes ten minutes to fill in." 3. Make a simple first version. Use a free design or spreadsheet tool. 4. Test it. Give it to three people and ask for honest feedback. 5. Improve it. Fix what confused them. 6. Create a preview. Show a mockup so people can see what they will get. 7. Choose a platform to sell it. Many marketplaces and payment tools exist. Check fees, rules and which options work in your country. 8. Write a clear description. What it is, who it is for, what is included and how to use it. 9. Set a fair price. Research similar products. 10. Share it with your audience honestly. Teach, show it in action and invite people to find out more.

For a detailed walk-through, read How To Create And Sell A Digital Product. If you decide to grow this into a business, How To Start And Grow A Profitable Digital Product Business goes further.

Selling from Instagram

  • Teach in your posts and invite people to message a keyword for the link.
  • Add your product to your link in bio and highlights.
  • Show real examples and honest results, such as screenshots with permission.
  • Answer questions in comments and stories.
  • Share customer feedback, with permission.

Never copy templates or designs from others. Check licences for fonts, images and icons, and read the rules for any marketplace you use. Be honest about what your product does and does not do. Offer clear refund terms where the platform requires them.

19Route Six: Your Own Handmade Or Physical Products

If you make something, such as jewellery, hair accessories, candles, baked goods or clothing, Instagram works as a shop window. Post clear photos and short videos, show your process, collect customer reviews and invite people to order by direct message or through a link.

Think carefully about practical matters: pricing that covers your materials, time and delivery, how you will take payments safely, how you will pack and ship, and any rules about selling your type of product in your country. Food, cosmetics and children's items often have specific safety and registration rules, so check them before you sell. Start small and learn before you scale.

20Route Seven: Platform Payments

Instagram has offered several ways for some creators to earn directly, such as gifts or subscriptions, depending on country and account eligibility. These tools change often, and some may not be available to you. Look in your professional account settings and Instagram's help pages for current options. Treat any platform payment as a bonus, not your whole plan, because rules, eligibility and payout terms can change quickly.

21Route Eight: Teaching And Coaching

If you have a skill, experience or result others want, you can teach it, in one-to-one sessions, group workshops or small programmes. Instagram helps people see how you think, so they trust you before they pay.

How to begin

  • Share helpful tips regularly so your audience sees your expertise.
  • Offer a small, low-priced first session or workshop to test demand.
  • Ask participants for feedback and a testimonial.
  • Gradually create a clear package, such as a four-week programme.

Please be careful in sensitive areas. Do not offer medical, legal, mental health or financial advice unless you are qualified and permitted to do so where you live. Stick to what you can honestly teach, and be clear about what you cannot do.

22Build Your Money Plan

You now know the eight routes. The mistake beginners make is trying all of them at once. Here is how to build a plan that stacks gently.

The stack idea

A stack means combining a few income streams so that you are not depending on one. A typical beginner stack, built over several months:

1. First stream (month one to three): a service or UGC, because they pay soonest. 2. Second stream (month three to six): affiliate links and small brand partnerships, as trust grows. 3. Third stream (month six onward): a digital product or coaching, once you know your audience's real questions.

The money maths

Let us demystify the numbers. Here are some made-up examples of how small streams can add up. Please research real prices in your market, because these figures are for teaching only.

StreamExampleWhat you need
Service3 monthly clients at a modest monthly fee3 clients
UGC4 projects a month at a modest fee each4 projects
Brand partnership1 small paid post a month1 deal
AffiliateA few commissions from honest recommendationsContent that helps
Digital productA low-priced template sold repeatedlySteady sales

Choose your numbers and work backwards. If your goal is to earn a set amount a month, how many clients, projects or sales do you need? How many messages and posts does that require? A frightening goal becomes a weekly checklist.

Work backwards

Take a monthly goal. Divide it by your average price to find how many sales you need. Assume you win one in ten pitches or conversations. Multiply to find how many people you must contact. For example, if you need four paid projects and win one in ten pitches, you need about forty pitches, which is about ten a week or two a working day.

A made-up example

Take Efua, a made-up example. She has about two thousand followers and posts about study tips. In month one she creates three UGC samples for study tools she already owns. In month two she pitches twenty small brands and gets two paid UGC jobs. In month three she adds an affiliate link for a planner she genuinely uses and offers a revision timetable template. By month six she has a handful of small income streams, none huge, which together cover her data, her subscriptions and a bit more. The first jump came from UGC, not from her follower count.

Track your income and expenses

Keep a simple spreadsheet: date, source, what for, amount, when you were paid and any expenses. Expenses may include tools, platform fees and gear. Keep invoices and receipts in a folder. Check your country's rules about reporting income and taxes. For a beginner's lesson, read Budget Like A Queen.

23Build Your Email List And Your Own Space

Instagram is rented land. Rules change, accounts can be limited and algorithms shift. If your income depends entirely on one platform, you are vulnerable. A simple way to protect yourself is to build something you own.

Start an email list

An email list is a list of people who have given you permission to email them. Offer a small free gift, such as a checklist or a short guide, in exchange for an email address. Use a free email tool, and read the rules about collecting emails and sending messages in your country, which often require clear consent and an easy way to unsubscribe.

Send a short, useful email regularly. People on your list are more likely to buy, and you will not lose them if the algorithm changes.

Keep a simple home base

A basic page with your story, your offers and your contact details gives brands and clients somewhere to land. It can be a one-page site or a link page. Keep it tidy and update it regularly.

Do not put all your eggs in one basket

Consider sharing your best ideas on a second platform too, so that if one changes, you have another route. See The Soft Girl's Guide To Becoming A Full-Time YouTube Creator and Personal Branding For Beginners for ideas.

24Where To Go: Finding Brands, Clients And Collaborators

Instagram is where people see you, but it is not the only place you will find opportunities. Think of it as your shop window and these other places as the streets that lead people to it. You do not need all of them. Choose your warm network, plus two or three others, and stay consistent for at least a month.

Your warm network (start here)

Your warm network is everyone who already knows you: friends, family, classmates, former colleagues, neighbours and community groups. Many first opportunities come from here, because trust already exists. A friend's cousin who runs a shop, a church member with a small business or a former classmate starting a brand can all be first clients.

A simple message: "Hi Zainab, I have started helping small businesses with their Instagram content, such as posts, captions and short videos. If you know anyone who might need a hand, I would love an introduction. I would be happy to do a small sample first."

Do not pressure anyone. Ask for introductions, not favours.

Instagram itself

Use Instagram to find and connect:

  • Search hashtags, locations and keywords related to businesses you could help.
  • Follow brands you would genuinely like to work with and engage with their posts thoughtfully before you ever pitch.
  • Join conversations on posts in your niche. Be helpful, not spammy.
  • Use direct messages respectfully for short, personal introductions.
  • Collaborate with creators at a similar level through shared posts, challenges or live conversations. Mutual support grows both accounts.

LinkedIn

LinkedIn is a professional network, and many marketing managers, founders and recruiters use it. Create a profile that clearly states your service, such as "Social media and UGC creator for small beauty brands." Connect with business owners and marketing people in your niche, share short lessons and message people politely. It is excellent for finding more established brands. See Babe, Your Next International Opportunity Is On LinkedIn.

X (formerly Twitter)

X is fast and public. Follow brand managers and founders in your niche, share short tips and reply thoughtfully. Some creators find clients by being visibly helpful. Keep your profile professional.

Facebook groups

Look for groups for small business owners in your area or niche, and groups for creators. Read the rules, help others and share your work only where self-promotion is allowed. Avoid groups full of "get rich quick" posts.

TikTok

Many creators use TikTok to reach people who might later follow them on Instagram. Short, genuine videos about your niche can bring new audiences. Check each platform's rules before reposting content, and remember that platform features and music rules differ.

Pinterest

Pinterest is a search engine for ideas. Pins that link to your website, blog or products can bring steady traffic over time, especially in niches like food, home, fashion, weddings, planning and design. It rewards patience and clear, searchable titles.

Reddit

Reddit communities for creators, freelancers and small businesses can be useful for learning and sometimes finding work. Read each community's rules carefully, because many ban self-promotion. Contribute honestly and avoid spamming.

Marketplaces and job boards

Some websites connect brands with creators and freelancers, and others list freelance and remote jobs. Create a clear profile, apply with personalised messages and read the platform's rules and fees. Be wary of any listing that asks you to pay before you work.

Local and in-person

Do not forget your own community. Local shops, salons, restaurants, schools, clinics, churches and markets often want help with their social media. A friendly visit, a printed card or a short introduction can open doors that no algorithm can.

How to choose

Ask: Where do the brands and clients I want to reach already spend time? Where can I show up weekly without dreading it? Pick your warm network, Instagram and one or two others.

25Scripts You Can Copy

A script removes the blank-screen panic. Every example is made up. Change the details until it sounds like you.

The kind and legal way to reach out

Be respectful. Write individual, personal messages, not copy-paste blasts. Say who you are and why you are writing to this person. Make it easy to say no, and stop if someone asks you to. Rules about unsolicited emails, direct messages and automated messaging differ by country and by platform, so check them. Instagram also limits spammy behaviour, so keep outreach small, genuine and personal.

Script one: a first direct message to a small business

"Hi Mrs Bello, I have been following your boutique for a while and love your ankara collection. I noticed it has been a few weeks since the last post. I create and schedule Instagram content for small businesses, and I would love to put together three sample posts for you, free, so you can see whether it helps. Would you be open to that? No pressure at all."

Keep it short. Mention something specific. Offer a small, clear step.

Script two: a first email to a brand for a collaboration

Subject: Collaboration idea for [Brand Name]

"Hello [Name],

I am Ruth, a creator who shares simple skincare tips for dry skin with about [number] followers, mostly women in their twenties. I have used your moisturiser for a few weeks and genuinely like how it feels, and my audience often asks for gentle product suggestions.

I would love to create a short video and a set of stories featuring your product, with honest feedback and clear disclosure. My media kit is attached with my audience details and past work.

Would you be open to a conversation about a paid collaboration? Thank you for your time.

Warm regards, Ruth Eze [handle] | [email]"

Notice that it is honest, specific and mentions the audience, not just the follower count.

Script three: a UGC pitch with samples

"Hello [Name], I create short, honest product videos for small brands, and I would love to make some for [Brand]. Here are three sample videos I made with products I own: [link]. If you like the style, I could create a short video with a hook, demonstration and caption for you to use on your own channels. I can share my rates and what is included. Would you like me to send details?"

Script four: a reply when a brand is interested

"Thank you so much for getting back to me! I would love to work together. To make sure I do this properly, could you tell me what you would like, by when and where the content will be used? I will send a short summary and my rates so we are both clear."

Script five: sharing your rates

"Thank you for your patience. For one short video with captions, delivered in five days with one round of changes, my fee is [amount]. This includes use on your organic social channels for [number] months. If you would like to use it in paid adverts or for longer, I can send a quote for extended usage. I would also need a paid partnership label on my post if it goes on my account. Would you like to proceed on those terms?"

Script six: negotiating politely

"Thank you for the offer, I appreciate it. My usual fee for this scope is [amount]. If the budget is fixed, I could adjust the project, for example by delivering one video instead of two, or shortening the usage period. Would either option work for you?"

Script seven: a follow-up

Send one follow-up about five to seven days after your first message.

"Hi [Name], I wanted to follow up on my note from last week in case it got buried. No worries if the timing is not right. Thank you again for your time."

If there is no reply, let it go for now. You can try again in a month with something new to share.

Script eight: declining a deal that is not right

"Thank you for thinking of me. After reading the details, I do not think this is the right fit for my audience, so I will pass. I appreciate the opportunity and would love to hear about future collaborations."

Saying no politely keeps doors open and protects your reputation with your audience.

Script nine: a reply to a free-product request that expects a lot

"Thank you for offering to send your product! I would love to try it. To be clear, a gifted product is not a guarantee of a post, and if I decide to feature it, I will disclose that it was gifted. If you are looking for guaranteed content, I would be happy to send my paid rates."

Script ten: asking for a testimonial

"I am so glad you are happy with the work! Would you be willing to write two or three sentences about your experience? It would mean a lot and help other businesses decide whether to work with me. I can send a few questions to make it easier."

Script eleven: a direct message sales reply for your own product

When someone messages you a keyword for your product link:

"Hi! Thank you for your interest in the budget planner. It is a spreadsheet you can use on your phone or computer, with a monthly view and a savings tracker. Here is the link: [link]. If you have any questions, I am happy to help."

Keep it friendly and honest. Do not pressure anyone.

Script twelve: collaborating with another creator

"Hi [Name], I love your content on [topic]. I think our audiences overlap nicely. Would you be interested in doing a simple collaboration, such as a shared reel or a live chat on [topic]? I would be glad to share ideas. No pressure at all."

Tracking your outreach

Open a spreadsheet with columns: date, name, platform, what I offered, reply, next step and follow-up date. Updating it daily turns a stressful task into a calm routine, and shows you which scripts and platforms work for you.

Pause For A Second 🌸 Please remember that most messages will not get a reply, and that is normal. Silence is not a verdict on your worth. It means timing, budget or fit was not right. Keep sending thoughtful messages, and keep improving.

26Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Everyone makes these. Seeing them in advance saves you months.

Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake one is chasing followers instead of trust. A small audience that listens beats a large one that scrolls past.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake two is posting without a niche. If nobody can tell what your account is for, nobody can follow it, and brands cannot picture working with you.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake three is buying followers, likes or comments. It destroys engagement and your credibility.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake four is waiting until you have a big following to start earning. Services and UGC work with small accounts.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake five is accepting free products as if they were payment. Gifts can be fine, but do not confuse them with income.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake six is hiding or forgetting disclosure. It breaks trust and can break rules.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake seven is working without written terms. A short written agreement prevents most disputes.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eight is posting inconsistently. Choose a rhythm you can keep and protect it.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake nine is copying other creators too closely. Be inspired, then bring your own voice.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake ten is giving up after a few quiet weeks. Most accounts that earn were quiet for months first.

27When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
I post but nobody sees itNew account, unclear niche or weak hooksSharpen your niche, improve your hooks, post reels and engage with others daily
I get views but no followersContent entertains but does not show who you areAdd a clear profile, a strong bio and a call to follow for more of a specific topic
I have followers but no engagementPassive or mismatched audienceAsk questions, reply to every comment and focus content on your ideal follower
Brands do not replyMessage too generic or sent to the wrong brandsPersonalise, mention a specific product, show samples and contact more suitable brands
Brands reply but ask for free workWrong kind of brand, or no rates yetShare your rate card, offer a small limited sample if you choose and be ready to decline
I get offers that seem too goodPossible scamVerify the brand, never pay to collaborate and follow the safety steps below
I feel burnt outUnsustainable postingReduce frequency, batch content and take planned breaks
My reach suddenly droppedAlgorithm changes or a content shiftReview insights, return to what worked and avoid panic
My account was restrictedPossible rule breach or suspicious activityRead the notice, follow Instagram's appeal steps and review your behaviour
I do not know what to postNo idea bankUse the idea sources, answer questions and repurpose old content
I am comparing myself constantlyNormal, but drainingMute accounts that make you feel small and track your own progress instead
I have no timePacked scheduleProtect two short fixed blocks a week and batch content

28Scam And Safety Warnings

I want you to be hopeful and careful at the same time. As soon as you start getting attention online, scammers notice.

Common scams aimed at creators

  • Fake brand deals. A "brand" offers a high-paying collaboration but asks you to pay first for a product, a "registration fee" or a "verification."
  • Fake cheque and overpayment scams. You are sent a payment larger than agreed and asked to return the difference. The original payment later proves fake.
  • Fake "verification" or "copyright" messages. A message claiming to be from Instagram says your account will be deleted unless you click a link or share a code. Instagram does not ask for your password by message.
  • Phishing links. Links that lead to fake login pages to steal your password.
  • Fake follower and engagement services. They take your money, damage your account and sometimes steal your login.
  • Pay-to-collaborate schemes. You are told you must pay to be featured or to join a "creator programme."
  • Pyramid and "easy money" schemes. Offers to earn big by recruiting others or by "liking and sharing."
  • Account takeover attempts. Someone pretends to be a friend or a brand and asks you to click or send a code.
  • Fake giveaways. Posts that ask you to share personal details or pay a "delivery fee."

Warning signs

Urgency and pressure. Requests for passwords, codes or payments. Offers that seem far too generous for your size. Messages from accounts with very few posts, odd handles or poor spelling. Requests to move to unusual chat apps. Anyone asking you to ignore agreements or contracts.

Safety habits

Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification. Never share login codes. Verify brands independently by checking their official website and contacting them through details published there, not through a link in the message. Do not pay to be paid. Keep payments and agreements documented. Report suspicious accounts and messages through the app. Trust the uneasy feeling in your stomach.

If you think you have been scammed

Please do not blame yourself. Clever people get tricked every day. Stop contact. Change your passwords immediately, starting with your email, and turn on two-step verification. Use Instagram's help pages to secure or recover your account. Contact your bank or payment provider quickly if you lost money. Save screenshots and details. Report it to the platform and to the authorities in your country. And tell someone you trust, because scammers rely on shame.

29Worked Examples

Let us walk through three made-up examples so you can see how the pieces fit. They are teaching examples, not real results.

Example one: Ruth, services through Instagram

Week one. Ruth enjoys design and wants income soon. She chooses services. Her one-line focus: "I help small salons keep their Instagram pages active and attractive so that they stay visible to local customers." She sets up a professional account, writes a clear bio and creates highlights for "Work with me" and "Results."

Weeks two to four. She designs three practice sets for fictional salons and posts them as samples. She posts two short tips a week about salon content.

Weeks five to eight. She builds a list of fifty local salons. She sends five personalised direct messages a day, offering three sample posts. About fifteen reply. Six want samples. Two become paying clients at a modest monthly fee.

Months three and four. She asks both for testimonials and shares them with permission. She raises her price for new clients and signs a third from a referral.

Lessons. One clear offer, steady outreach, small limited samples and testimonials.

Example two: Efua, UGC with a small account

Week one. Efua has fewer than two thousand followers and enjoys filming. She chooses UGC and writes her focus: "I make honest, simple product videos for small study and stationery brands."

Weeks two to three. She films three practice videos using her own notebooks, pens and a planner. She learns to use natural light and clear sound.

Weeks four to eight. She makes a short portfolio page and contacts twenty small stationery brands with her samples. A few reply, and two offer small paid UGC projects.

Months three to five. She delivers on time, collects feedback, raises her prices slightly and adds a revision timetable template to sell.

Lessons. UGC does not need a big following. It needs samples, reliability and persistence.

Example three: Amaka, a niche account building brand deals and affiliate income

Week one. Amaka loves skincare for dry skin and has about three thousand followers. She focuses on honest reviews and routines.

Weeks two to eight. She posts three reels and a carousel each week. She replies to comments daily and tracks insights weekly. She notices that carousel posts about ingredients get the most saves, so she makes more.

Months three to four. She creates a simple media kit with honest figures and contacts fifteen small skincare brands, with a personal note and a sample video. A few reply. One offers a small paid collaboration and a few offer gifted products, which she accepts only when she genuinely wants them, and discloses clearly.

Months five to eight. She joins an affiliate programme for products she really uses and shares helpful content. She builds an email list with a free routine checklist. Over time, her income is a mix of small brand deals, affiliate commissions and occasional UGC.

Lessons. A clear niche, honest content, clear disclosure and patience.

Create your own example

Write your own story in five lines: Who I want to reach. What I will offer. How I will find people. What I will do in my first thirty days. What I will review in ninety days.

30Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

When you start creating, familiar voices appear. Here is how I answer them.

"Who am I to post this?" You are someone who knows something that a person a few steps behind you needs to hear. You do not need to be the greatest in the world.

"Everyone is doing this already." Yes, and people still need your voice, your angle and your honesty. Nobody else can be you.

"I have too few followers." Many opportunities, such as services and UGC, do not depend on follower count. Start with what you have.

"What if people laugh at me?" Some may, and most will not notice. The people who matter will be the ones who need what you share.

"I feel like I am failing." You are comparing your day three with someone's year five. Compare yourself with last month's you.

"I do not have time." You do not need hours. Thirty focused minutes most days is enough to make progress.

"What if I never earn?" You may learn a lot of valuable skills along the way, such as content creation, communication and selling, which help in many careers. And you will find out sooner than if you never tried.

You are not behind. You are building something in public, one post at a time.

31Your First Seven Days: A Gentle Quick Start

About thirty to sixty minutes a day.

Day 1. Write your one-line focus and choose your starting route.

Day 2. Switch to a professional account, set your username, name and photo and secure your account with two-step verification.

Day 3. Write your bio, link page and highlights.

Day 4. Do the niche worksheet, describe your ideal follower and list three content pillars.

Day 5. Create a bank of ten content ideas and write three strong hooks.

Day 6. Film or design your first two posts and write the captions.

Day 7. Post, reply to comments, leave five thoughtful comments on other accounts and review your first insights.

32Your Thirty-Day Plan

Here is a full month. About thirty to sixty minutes a day. If you miss a day, simply continue.

Week one: foundation

  • Days 1 to 7: follow the seven-day quick start above.

Week two: create and learn

  • Day 8: Plan a week of content using your pillars.
  • Day 9: Batch film or design three posts.
  • Day 10: Edit, add captions and schedule posts.
  • Day 11: Engage for twenty minutes: reply, comment and message.
  • Day 12: Make a carousel that teaches one idea.
  • Day 13: Review your insights and note what is working.
  • Day 14: Plan next week using what you learned.

Week three: prepare to earn

  • Day 15: Write your service offer or UGC rate card.
  • Day 16: Create three practice samples.
  • Day 17: Build your simple portfolio page or folder.
  • Day 18: Build a simple media kit with honest numbers.
  • Day 19: Make a list of twenty brands or businesses that fit.
  • Day 20: Write personal notes for the first ten.
  • Day 21: Review and refine your samples.

Week four: reach out and track

  • Day 22: Send five personal messages and track them.
  • Day 23: Send five more.
  • Day 24: Follow up on week three's conversations.
  • Day 25: Send five more, and join one community or group.
  • Day 26: Reply to interest, share rates and send a written summary.
  • Day 27: Offer one small, limited sample if you choose.
  • Day 28: Keep posting and engaging.
  • Day 29: Review your numbers: posts, messages, replies and conversations.
  • Day 30: Write your next thirty-day goal.

33Your Ninety-Day Plan

Days 1 to 30: foundation and first outreach

Complete the thirty-day plan. By day thirty you should have a clear niche, a tidy profile, a content rhythm, a small portfolio, a media kit or service offer and your first messages sent.

Days 31 to 60: consistency and conversations

Post consistently. Send two to five personal messages a day. Hold conversations and offer small, limited samples. Deliver well and ask for testimonials. Join one affiliate programme for a product you truly use, if it fits your niche.

Days 61 to 90: earn and refine

Focus on turning samples into paid work and one-off work into repeat work. Raise your prices slightly after each success. Consider a small digital product based on questions you are asked often. Review your numbers and your energy: what worked, what drained you and what you will do more of.

Monthly check-in questions

  • How many posts did I publish, and which performed best?
  • How many people did I contact?
  • How many replied?
  • How many conversations or deals did I have?
  • How much did I earn, and how much did I spend?
  • What did I enjoy, and what drained me?
  • What will I do more of, less of or differently next month?

34Questions Girls Ask Me

Can I really make money on Instagram with a small following?

Many people earn through services, UGC and small brand partnerships without a big following. I cannot promise results, and what you earn depends on your niche, skills, effort, country and timing. What I can say is that clarity and consistency matter more than raw numbers.

How many followers do I need?

There is no magic number. For services and UGC, you may need very few. For some brand deals, brands care about your engagement and audience fit as much as your size. Smaller, engaged accounts can be valuable.

How long does it take to earn something?

Often a few months of consistent work before a first small paid opportunity, but it varies a lot. Some people are faster and many are slower.

Do I need to show my face?

No. Many creators show their hands, their products or their screen, or use voiceovers and graphics. Some brands and clients prefer a face, so choose what you are comfortable with.

Do I need a business account?

Professional accounts offer useful tools such as insights, so most people who want to earn switch to one. Check current options in your settings.

How do I know how much to charge?

Think about your time, the deliverables, usage rights, exclusivity and the market. Start with a fair, modest price and raise it as your skill and proof grow. The free Freelance Rate Calculator can help.

Should I accept free products?

Only if you genuinely want the product and are happy to talk about it honestly. Gifted items are not income, and you still need to disclose them according to the rules where you live.

Do I have to disclose partnerships?

In many countries, yes. Use Instagram's paid partnership tools and clear wording, and check your local advertising rules.

How do I deal with a brand that does not pay?

Keep all your communication and agreements in writing, send a polite reminder, then a firmer one, and consider your options under your agreement and local rules. Prevention helps: agree on terms and deposits upfront.

How do I avoid scams?

Verify brands independently, never pay to be paid, never share passwords or codes and be cautious about urgent requests. When in doubt, walk away.

How often should I post?

As often as you can keep up with for months. For many people, three to five posts a week plus stories is a good starting point. Consistency beats intensity.

What should I do after my first paid project?

Deliver beautifully, ask for a testimonial and a referral, raise your prices gradually and build your next stream. Then keep going.

36What To Do Next

You have reached the end of a long guide, and that tells me something lovely about you: you take your goals seriously and you are willing to learn.

Here is what I want you to keep. Instagram does not pay you for being perfect or famous. It gives you a place to be seen by people who might need what you can offer. The women who earn there are usually not the most talented or the most followed. They are the ones who chose a clear niche, showed up consistently, treated brands and followers with honesty and kept going through the quiet months.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, write your one-line focus. Tomorrow, tidy your profile and secure your account. This week, post something useful and send your first thoughtful message. In a month, look back and notice how different your account feels.

When it is slow, remember that slow is still moving. When someone says no, thank them and move on. When someone says yes, deliver beautifully.

When you are ready for more, here are good next steps. Personal Branding For Beginners helps people remember who you are. How To Get Your First Freelance Client deepens the services route. How To Create And Sell A Digital Product turns your knowledge into a product. The Soft Girl's Guide To Becoming A Full-Time YouTube Creator explores a second platform. And 35 Income Streams That Can Become Semi-Passive shows what you can build over time.

I am rooting for you, sis. Begin tonight, go gently and keep going.
